title: SYSK Selects: How Haunted House Attractions Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of a 2014 episode on how haunted house attractions work. Josh and Chuck cover the history from ancient Egypt grave traps, Greek and Roman mazes, medieval scare plays, Shakespeare, Victorian wax museums and Pepper's ghost, through early dark rides and the 1915 Edwardian Fair ghost house, Disneyland's Haunted Mansion, and the Junior Chamber (j c's) fundraiser haunted houses of the 1970s. They then discuss the modern industry (commercial, charity and home haunts, Halloween spending stats), how operators run flow and throughput, scare forward tactics, compressed-air effects, the 2000s safety lessons after the Six Flags Great Adventure fire, extreme haunts like McKamey Manor, and church-run hell houses. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about The Karate Kid.
topics: Junior Chamber of Commerce haunted houses
Six Flags Great Adventure haunted house fire

segments.title: Opening banter and haunted house overview
segments.summary: Josh introduces the rerun and the hosts discuss that haunted houses are widespread, including commercial, charity and home haunts, and cite 2014 National Retail Federation figures on attendance and Halloween spending.

segments.title: Ancient and early history of scare attractions
segments.summary: The hosts trace early precursors: ancient Egyptian grave traps, Greek and Roman mazes and stage effects, medieval Dark Ages scare plays, Shakespeare's ghosts and monsters, and Victorian wax museums and spiritualism.

segments.title: Dark rides and the first haunted attractions
segments.summary: Pepper's ghost uses mirrors to create ghostly illusions. Twentieth-century dark rides were cheap painted dark buildings with pop-out scares. The hosts cite the 1915 Edwardian Fair ghost house as an early genuine haunted attraction and note the Disneyland Haunted Mansion opened in 1969 as a dark ride after a walkthrough version had flow problems.

segments.title: Junior Chamber of Commerce haunted house fundraisers
segments.summary: The US Junior Chamber (j c's) created the first annual American haunted house fundraisers in the 1970s, and a Bloomington, Illinois chapter's members formed the Haunted House Company to sell plans. Commercial haunts grew in the 1990s, with examples such as Another World in Atlanta and Thirteenth Story in New Orleans.

segments.title: Movie talk and themed haunts
segments.summary: Hosts discuss horror movies they like, including The Woman in Black and directors of The Innkeepers and House of the Devil, then describe haunt themes and Rob Zombie's Great American Nightmare, including a room tied to John Wayne Gacy.

segments.title: Running a haunted house: business, safety and flow
segments.summary: Operators need business skills and budget for decorations and effects. The 1980s Six Flags Great Adventure modular haunted dark ride fire killed eight teenagers, prompting safety changes. A 2011 Creepy World employee was caught in a noose and survived with brain damage. Throughput is managed so groups don't bump, and scare forward keeps guests moving ahead.

segments.title: Extreme haunted attractions and hell houses
segments.summary: Extreme haunts like McKamey Manor in San Diego involve physical contact, confinement and long sessions, with waivers. Hell houses are church-run attractions that depict sins such as abortion and drug use, ending in Hell and a call to repentance; the format originated with Jerry Falwell in the 1970s and was later packaged for sale.

segments.title: BuzzFeed scared faces and closing
segments.summary: Josh recommends BuzzFeed's photo collection of people's scared faces at haunted attractions and wraps up the topic.

segments.title: Listener mail: The Karate Kid
segments.summary: A listener writes about enjoying the earlier Karate Kid episode and sharing the film with a nephew, and mentions a cover of The Best Around by the Bangalore's.
